chapters.title: Aliasing: what a 24 fps camera does to a puffing flame
chapters.what: A buoyant flame puffs at about f ≈ 1.5/√D (D in metres). A camera that takes fs pictures per second can only represent frequencies up to the Nyquist limit fs/2; anything faster is folded back into [0, fs/2] and looks like a slower oscillation. At 23.976 fps the limit is 11.99 Hz, and an 11.6 mm burner puffs at about 14 Hz, just above it.
chapters.looks: Blue: the true oscillation. Amber dots: what the camera records, one per frame. Rose dashed: the slower sine that passes through every dot, which is the frequency an analysis of the video would report. 3D: the apparent frequency as a saw-tooth surface over true f and fs.
chapters.change: Drag f upward through 11.99 Hz and watch the rose curve turn around; raise fs to 120 and the fold vanishes. ▶ sweeps f from 1 to 40 Hz.
chapters.use: Reading frequencies from phone or DSLR video; choosing a frame rate before an experiment; deciding which diagnostics (permutation entropy, 0-1 test) survive aliasing and which (spectral peak positions) do not.
misc: Aliasing does not add noise: the folded sine fits the samples exactly, which is why it cannot be detected from the video alone.
Raising the frame rate fixes it; filtering after the fact cannot.

chapters.title: Veiling glare and the threshold: measuring the flame, not the halo
chapters.what: A very bright flame against a dark room scatters light inside the lens: a smooth halo surrounds it. A fixed grey-level threshold then measures the halo, not the flame (on the real MVI_8036 footage a fixed threshold overestimated the width 2.8–4.6×). FlameLab subtracts a heavily blurred copy of the frame (unsharp-mask glare correction) and re-chooses the threshold in every frame with Otsu's method.
chapters.looks: A single row through the flame: blue is the raw frame (flame plus halo), green the glare-corrected row. The amber line is a fixed threshold, the rose line is Otsu's threshold on the corrected row; grey dotted lines are the true edges. 3D: the intensity of the axisymmetric flame as a surface.
chapters.change: Raise the glare fraction g or the halo width and the amber threshold crosses the halo far outside the flame; the corrected, Otsu-thresholded width stays on the true edge. Set α = 0 to see that correction and thresholding are separate steps.
chapters.use: Any bright-source metrology: flame height and width, lamps, sparks, laser spots. The reason a flame video cannot be thresholded by eye.
misc: Glare is not noise: averaging many frames does not remove it.
Even after correction 'where the flame ends' is partly a convention, so FlameLab also reports a systematic uncertainty.

chapters.title: Sub-pixel edges: reading a boundary to a tenth of a pixel
chapters.what: A pixel only says 'above or below the threshold', so an integer-pixel edge is wrong by a uniformly distributed amount (standard deviation 1/√12 ≈ 0.29 px). If the true edge is blurred over a pixel or more, the pixel values on either side carry the position: interpolate linearly to where the profile crosses the threshold. FlameLab does this for every row of the flame contour.
chapters.looks: Error of the detected edge as the true edge slides across one pixel. Amber: integer-pixel detection, a saw-tooth. Teal: sub-pixel interpolation. Dots: the current offset.
chapters.change: Increase the blur σ: the profile becomes more linear and the sub-pixel error shrinks. Make the edge sharper (σ → 0.2): interpolation has nothing to work with and helps much less. Add noise: both degrade, interpolation still wins.
chapters.use: Calibrated lengths from pixel images; the reason flame length is determined far better than one pixel; edge metrology in microscopy and machine vision.
misc: Sub-pixel does not mean sub-pixel accurate: a biased threshold or glare shifts the edge by more than the interpolation gains.
A perfectly sharp edge cannot be located below the pixel; a little blur helps.

chapters.title: The kymograph: stripe slope is convection speed
chapters.what: Stack the flame's left and right edge (or its intensity along the axis) for every frame: you get an image with height up and time across. A structure that is born at the base and rises at speed U draws a straight stripe z = U(t − t₀). The slope of the stripes is the convection speed and their spacing in time is the puffing period.
chapters.looks: Amber lines: the stripes of successive puffs. The rose arrow is the slope. 3D: the travelling wave sin(2πf(t − z/U)) as a surface over time and height.
chapters.change: Raise U: stripes steepen (the structure climbs faster). Raise f: stripes crowd together in time. Increase the tracking noise and watch the estimated speed drift.
chapters.use: Convection speed and puffing frequency from one image; checking optical-flow results; spotting pinch-off and merging events as stripe breaks.
misc: Regressing height on time shrinks the slope when the noise is in time (regression dilution); regress time on height and invert.
Real kymographs from this rig gave 4.5–5.9 mm/s, far below a buoyancy estimate: the stripes may track a slow envelope, not the vortices.

chapters.title: Flame height: Heskestad's correlation and the burning-rate proxy
chapters.what: The mean visible height of a turbulent diffusion flame depends on the heat release rate and the burner diameter through the dimensionless Q*. For Q* > 1 the height grows like Q^{2/5}, so a measured height gives back a burning-rate proxy: Q̇ ∝ L^{5/2}. FlameLab uses the proxy r = (L/L̄)^{5/2} to follow the ramp-up of a self-feeding pool flame.
chapters.looks: Height against heat release for this burner (amber) and for a burner 1.5× wider (dashed); the dot is your Q̇. 3D: height over (Q̇, D).
chapters.change: Raise Q̇ and the curve flattens (power 2/5). Widen D at fixed Q̇ and the flame gets shorter. Move L/L̄ to see how a 20 % longer flame means 58 % more burning.
chapters.use: Estimating heat release from video; comparing flames from different burners; converting flame-height time series to a burning-rate history.
misc: The correlation is a mean (intermittency 0.5) height; instantaneous heights fluctuate around it.
Q̇ here is the total heat release, not the fuel flow.

chapters.title: The onset of puffing: supercritical and subcritical Hopf bifurcation
chapters.what: Close to the onset of puffing the oscillation amplitude A obeys a normal form. If the cubic term saturates the growth (supercritical), the amplitude grows smoothly from zero at σ = 0 as σ rises. If the cubic term pushes the other way and a quintic term saturates it (subcritical), the flame can jump to a large puffing amplitude and stay there even for σ < 0 (hysteresis). The early growth rate σ, fitted to the amplitude of the real flame, tells them apart.
chapters.looks: Amplitude against time (teal), the early exponential fit (rose dashed) and the saturation level. 3D: dA/dt over (σ, A): the surface crosses zero where the amplitude is steady.
chapters.change: Raise σ and the amplitude saturates at √(σ/β) and the fit recovers σ. Switch to subcritical, set σ slightly negative and start from a large A₀: the amplitude stays high.
chapters.use: Classifying how a flame transitions to puffing; interpreting a growth-rate fit across the onset window of real video.
misc: A fitted growth rate needs the window where A is small but above the noise; fit too late and you measure the saturation.
Supercritical vs subcritical is a statement about the cubic term, not about how fast the growth is.

chapters.title: Inverse Abel transform by onion peeling
chapters.what: A camera sees a line-of-sight projection of the flame's emission. If the flame is axisymmetric, the radial emission profile ε(r) can be recovered from one view: peel the flame like an onion, outermost ring first. Each ring is solved from the chords that cross only rings already solved. The method is exact for the discrete model but amplifies noise strongly toward the axis.
chapters.looks: Blue: the projection (what the camera records, scaled). Dashed: the true emission. Rose: the recovered emission. 3D: the recovered axisymmetric field.
chapters.change: Increase N and the discretization error falls. Add noise and the recovered profile blows up near the centre.
chapters.use: Radial soot or temperature profiles of laminar flames, plasma jets and sprays from a single image.
misc: It needs axisymmetry; a flapping, puffing flame violates it.
Clipped (saturated) rows must be refused, not inverted.

chapters.title: Finding the onset of puffing: sliding band power and a change point
chapters.what: A flame record is not stationary: it grows, sits quietly, then starts to puff. A single spectrum of the whole record averages these stages together. Instead compute the fraction of spectral power above 5 Hz in a sliding window, then find the time where this feature steps up. The window length sets the time resolution: a longer window sees frequency better but smears the onset.
chapters.looks: Teal dots: the band-power fraction in each window. Grey line: the true onset. Rose line: the change point found by the single-step fit.
chapters.change: Lower the puffing amplitude until the step disappears into the noise. Lengthen the window and see the error grow. Move the puffing frequency toward Nyquist.
chapters.use: Locating regime changes in time series: ignition, onset of instability, transition.
misc: A single step model finds one onset; a record with several regimes needs multiple change points or an HMM.
The detected time is a window centre: it carries ± half a window of uncertainty.

chapters.title: Stitching video parts: one frame stream, honest bookkeeping
chapters.what: A long recording is often saved as several files. FlameLab can read them as one continuous stream, but only if three things hold: the parts have the same frame rate and size, no real time was lost between them, and the frame counts are measured, not read from the container headers (which can be wrong by a couple of frames per file, and every error shifts all later frames).
chapters.looks: Coloured boxes: the parts laid end to end on the global frame axis; vertical bars: the seams (amber if contiguous, rose if time was lost). Rose segments: how far every later part shifts if a header over-counts.
chapters.change: Introduce a gap or an fps mismatch and the verdict turns to REFUSED. Give the headers an error and the drift after the last seam grows with the number of parts.
chapters.use: Analysing a long burn recorded in chunks; joining parts without re-encoding; protecting spectral analysis from gaps.
misc: A joined file hides a gap: the timestamps become contiguous.
Re-muxing a stream copy can drop the last packets of each file; count packets, not headers.
